text: For transplanted lowland rice, use shallow water around transplanting rather than deep standing water. TNAU guidance describes about 2 cm of water at transplanting and for the first seven days after transplanting. Provide drainage so excess water can be removed.

Pay close attention to water availability in rice around panicle initiation, booting, heading and flowering. Avoid moisture stress at these important growth stages and maintain field drainage to manage excess water.

Base rice fertilizer decisions on a soil test and the variety, season and local recommendation. TNAU describes split nutrient application at crop stages such as tillering, panicle initiation and heading; avoid applying a blanket dose without checking local guidance.

Where suitable for the field and local system, alternate wetting and drying can be monitored with a field water tube. Follow a locally validated safe depletion threshold for the soil type rather than allowing the crop to experience severe water stress.

Inspect rice fields regularly for pests and disease symptoms. Keep field records, identify the problem before choosing a control measure, and use integrated pest management and locally recommended practices.
Maize is sensitive to both moisture shortage and excess water. Pay particular attention to adequate soil moisture during flowering and silking, and adjust irrigation to soil type and rainfall.
Provide drainage in maize fields after heavy rain because waterlogging can damage the crop. Check low-lying parts of the field and clear blocked drainage channels.

Monitor maize moisture conditions closely during the flowering phase. TNAU identifies approximately 45 to 65 days after sowing as a critical moisture period in its maize irrigation guidance; actual timing varies with variety and conditions.

Keep the maize crop free from heavy weed competition during early establishment. Use locally recommended cultural or mechanical weed control, and verify herbicide choice, crop stage and label directions with an agricultural extension officer.

Inspect maize plants regularly for leaf damage and signs of insect activity. Identify the pest correctly before selecting a management method, and follow integrated pest management advice from the local agriculture department.
Avoid moisture stress in wheat at important growth stages. TNAU lists crown root initiation, active tillering, flowering and grain filling among the stages to consider when planning irrigation.
Prevent water stagnation around wheat germination. Check field levelling and drainage after irrigation or rainfall so seedlings are not left in standing water.

Monitor wheat fields for weeds early in the crop cycle. Where herbicides are considered, confirm the weed species, crop stage, product registration and label directions with a qualified local adviser.
Plan wheat fertilizer application using soil test results and local recommendations. Match nitrogen timing to crop growth instead of applying extra fertilizer without checking crop need.
source_name: TNAU Agritech - Good Agricultural Practices for fertilizer use

text: Check grain maturity before harvesting wheat. TNAU describes harvesting when grains become hard and the straw is dry and brittle; confirm the right timing for the variety and local weather.
Tomato performs well in well-drained loamy soil with organic matter. TNAU gives a soil pH range of about 6.5 to 7.5 in its open-field tomato guidance; test the field soil before making amendments.
source_name: TNAU Agritech - Tomato soil and field preparation

text: After tomato seedlings establish, keep irrigation reasonably even and adjust it for soil, weather and crop stage. Avoid long dry periods followed by sudden heavy irrigation, which can contribute to fruit cracking.
source_name: TNAU Agritech - Organic tomato water requirements

text: Use healthy, well-grown tomato seedlings and prepare a well-drained field before transplanting. TNAU guidance describes transplanting seedlings around 25 days old and providing an establishment irrigation around the third day; adapt to local conditions.
source_name: TNAU Agritech - Tomato soil and field preparation

text: Tomato plants may benefit from staking or training, especially when plants carry fruit. Support can make field operations and harvesting easier; use a method suited to the variety and production system.

Use soil-test-based nutrient management for tomato. Fertilizer needs vary by variety, soil and production system, so do not copy a fertigation or fertilizer schedule from another farm without local advice.
